disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through learning of such events affecting close others. It is characterized by intrusive re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity, all persisting for more than one month and causing clinically significant distress or functional impairment. The course can be chronic or fluctuating, with onset sometimes delayed, and it is distinguished from acute stress reactions by its duration and from primary mood or anxiety disorders by the centrality of a qualifying traumatic event and trauma-linked symptom clusters. Comorbidity with depression, substance use, and other anxiety disorders is common, and functional impact often emerges in interpersonal, occupational, or community roles.

narrative.stressor: Two years and three months ago, Heidi was leading an evening historic walking tour when a speeding pickup ran a red light in downtown Belvidere and struck a small group at the crosswalk, killing one teenage participant and severely injuring another she knew from the community garden. Although she was not physically injured, she was close enough to see the impact and stayed with the teens, trying to comfort them until emergency services arrived, later replaying the chaotic scene as she gave statements to police and local reporters. In the months that followed, she gradually withdrew from leading tours and avoided the intersection, but the impact of the incident seeped into other cherished routines at the senior center and church, straining her sense of purpose and connection. She finally agreed to see a mental health professional at the urging of her pastor and a longtime friend after they noticed she had stopped attending book club and bowling, and she admitted she could no longer enjoy the community activities that once defined her retirement.
narrative.chief_complaint: I just don’t feel any interest in the community projects and hobbies that used to mean everything to me.

narrative.stressor: About two years and three months ago, Lacedrick was walking home from an evening youth program at the church when a drive-by shooting erupted on his block; a teenage boy he knew from the basketball court was shot a few feet away from him, and Lacedrick dropped to the ground, believing he would be next. In the aftermath, he helped organize vigils and spoke out against gun violence, but privately he found that every trip past that corner and every late-night siren pulled him back into the terror of that night, even as he tried to maintain his role as a steady spiritual leader. Over time, his difficulty staying present during services, planning youth activities in that neighborhood, and riding the subway after dark began to interfere with both seminary work and church responsibilities, forcing him to cancel commitments and lean on others to cover for him. When an older pastor gently confronted him about his growing avoidance of certain ministry tasks and his visible tension during community events, Lacedrick agreed to seek psychiatric help, saying he could no longer keep functioning in his calling while feeling constantly on edge.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like I’m always on guard and tense, like something bad is about to happen every time I’m out in the neighborhood.

narrative.stressor: Two years and three months ago, Jenny was driving home from a late catering event on a rural stretch of road near the Natchez Trace when a drunk driver crossed the center line and slammed into the side of her car, trapping her until first responders cut her out of the vehicle; she later learned that the other driver died at the scene. Initially focused on her physical recovery and the logistics of insurance and car replacement, she tried to return to her busy routine of dance classes, trail runs, and pop-up food events, but found herself rearranging routes and turning down jobs that required driving at night or on highways. As time went on, her reluctance to travel for catering gigs, join friends for hikes that involved carpooling, or even ride as a passenger began to erode her business plans and social life, leaving her more isolated than her usually spontaneous, outgoing self. After her mother pointed out how much her world had shrunk and Jenny realized she was postponing her dream of expanding the catering business because of it, she agreed to see a psychiatrist to understand why she couldn’t seem to move past the crash.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve started going out of my way to avoid driving or being in cars, and it’s taking over my life.
